# Why the antecedent temperature window was replaced

```{r a2-load}
D2 <- rev_tab("D2_within_reach_window_change.csv")
D3 <- rev_tab("D3_shuffled_date_null.csv")
D4 <- rev_tab("D4_comid_slope_vs_artifact.csv")
d3o <- D3 |> filter(run == "observed")
d3n <- D3 |> filter(run == "null_mean")
d2_90 <- D2 |> filter(window == "temp_90")
```

In the original submission, each redd's thermal covariate was the mean modeled temperature over the 90 days ending on that redd's own spawn date ("temp_90"). Because the window is anchored to the response, spawn date enters both sides of the model: any seasonal trend in stream temperature produces an association between spawn date and temp_90 even if spawning is unrelated to temperature. This appendix quantifies that artifact. The analyses are in `R/07_window-artifact-diagnostics.R`.

## Seasonal context

Stream temperature across surveyed reaches peaked in late July, and no redd was completed before the peak (@fig-a2-thermograph). A 90-day window ending in August or September therefore spans cold late-spring days at its start and warm summer days at its end. Moving the end date later drops cold days and adds warm ones, so a later spawn date mechanically yields a warmer temp_90.

```{r}
#| label: fig-a2-thermograph
#| fig-cap: "Network-mean modeled daily stream temperature for surveyed reaches, 2002–2005 (grey band: 10th–90th percentiles). Shaded: range of observed spawn dates; dashed line: thermal peak."
#| out-width: "80%"
knitr::include_graphics(rev_plot("D1_seasonal_thermograph.png"))
```

## Within a reach-year, the window re-codes the date

Redds in the same reach and year share the same stream; they differ only in spawn date. Within reach-years, temp_90 rose `r sprintf("%.2f", d2_90$change_per_10d)` °C for every 10 days of later spawning and was almost perfectly correlated with spawn date (r = `r sprintf("%.2f", d2_90$r_within)`; @tbl-a2-windows). The direction of the artifact depends on window length: a 30-d window ending in August sits on the summer peak and becomes *cooler* as it moves later, whereas the 90-d window becomes warmer. This explains why the 90-d window was the best predictor in the original screening, and why biologically more plausible shorter windows were not: only the 90-d artifact reinforces the spatial pattern.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-a2-windows
#| tbl-cap: "Change in date-anchored antecedent temperature with spawn date among redds in the same reach and year."
D2 |>
  transmute(
    Window = sub("temp_", "", window) |> paste0("-d antecedent mean"),
    `Change per 10 d later (°C)` = sprintf("%+.2f", change_per_10d),
    `r with date, within reach-year` = sprintf("%.2f", r_within),
    `r with date, raw` = sprintf("%.2f", r_raw),
    `Variance within reach-year` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * var_share_within)
  ) |>
  kbl2(align = "lrrrr")
```

## A null model with no biology

To ask how much of the original fit the artifact alone could produce, we shuffled spawn dates among redds within each year (200 permutations), recomputed temp_90 at each redd's own reach for its new date, and refit the models. Shuffling destroys any real link between a place's temperature and its spawn timing but keeps the window construction intact.

Random dates still produced R² = `r sprintf("%.2f", d3n$r2_quad)` for spawn date on temp_90 (quadratic; observed `r sprintf("%.2f", d3o$r2_quad)`), and a within-reach slope of `r sprintf("%.1f", d3n$within_slope_d_per_C)` d per °C, slightly steeper than observed (`r sprintf("%.1f", d3o$within_slope_d_per_C)`; @tbl-a2-null, @fig-a2-null). The mixed model fit to random dates predicted them with a residual SD of `r sprintf("%.1f", d3n$lmer_resid_sd)` d, against `r sprintf("%.1f", d3o$lmer_resid_sd)` d for the real data. The within-reach temperature response in the original model is therefore indistinguishable from the artifact; the real signal lies in temperature differences among reaches and years.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-a2-null
#| tbl-cap: "Observed fit statistics compared with 200 shuffled-date null datasets."
D3 |>
  filter(run %in% c("observed", "null_mean", "null_q025", "null_q975")) |>
  mutate(run = recode(run,
    observed = "Observed", null_mean = "Null, mean",
    null_q025 = "Null, 2.5%", null_q975 = "Null, 97.5%"
  )) |>
  transmute(
    ` ` = run,
    `R² (quadratic)` = sprintf("%.2f", r2_quad),
    `R² (+ stream + year)` = sprintf("%.2f", r2_quad_stream_year),
    `Within reach-year slope (d per °C)` = sprintf("%.1f", within_slope_d_per_C),
    `Mixed-model residual SD (d)` = sprintf("%.2f", lmer_resid_sd)
  ) |>
  kbl2(align = "lrrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-a2-null
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of fit statistics from 200 shuffled-date null datasets (grey) and the observed value (red)."
#| out-width: "90%"
knitr::include_graphics(rev_plot("D3_shuffled_date_null.png"))
```

## Reach-specific slopes reflect thermograph shape

If temp_90 rises at a rate of *b* °C per day within a reach-year, a regression of spawn date on temp_90 within that reach has slope 1/*b* days per °C regardless of biology. For the `r nrow(D4)` reaches with at least 15 redds, the observed within-reach slope tracked this artifact-only expectation (r = `r sprintf("%.2f", cor(D4$slope_observed, D4$slope_artifact))`; medians `r sprintf("%.1f", median(D4$slope_observed))` and `r sprintf("%.1f", median(D4$slope_artifact))` d per °C; @fig-a2-slopes). The reach-specific random slopes reported in the original submission ("thermal sensitivity") therefore largely describe how quickly each reach's 90-day mean warms through August, not how fish respond to temperature. The new analysis uses a thermal index that is fixed in calendar time (Section A3).

```{r}
#| label: fig-a2-slopes
#| fig-cap: "Observed within-reach slope of spawn date on temp_90 versus the slope expected from window construction alone (1 / rate at which the window warms), for reaches with at least 15 redds. Dashed line: 1:1."
#| out-width: "75%"
knitr::include_graphics(rev_plot("D4_comid_slope_vs_artifact.png"))
```
